body.text: Former Japanese Prime Minister Abe Shinzo first proposed the “Free and Open Indo-Pacific” (FOIP) in 2016. A decade on, the international environment is considerably more difficult. The United States’ high-tariff policies, China’s tightening of export controls on critical minerals, and the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz have all disrupted global supply chains. The threat of cyberattacks targeting the theft of classified information and the disabling of critical infrastructure has also intensified.

The “Updated FOIP” that the current Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae outlined in her Hanoi address of May 2026 is in part a response to these changed circumstances. While reaffirming the established principles of freedom, openness, diversity, inclusiveness, and the rule of law, the Updated FOIP brings to the fore each country’s “autonomy” and “resilience” as conditions for realizing the FOIP vision. Among the priority areas highlighted, the resilience of supply chains for energy and critical materials, and the development of infrastructure essential to the AI and data age, are directions that align closely with Japan’s own economic security policy.

The object of economic security is not economic decoupling from specific countries, nor self-sufficiency; it is to reduce vulnerability to supply disruptions and similar shocks while preserving the benefits of international division of labor, thereby limiting losses to society as a whole. Where procurement of critical materials is heavily concentrated in a single country with few alternatives, for instance, that dependence can be exploited for economic coercion. At the same time, when companies choose their suppliers, they do not always fully account for the broader societal losses their own supply disruption might cause. Nor do governments necessarily give adequate weight to the impact of their decisions on other countries, as they tend to prioritize national interests.

In practice, during the COVID-19 pandemic and again during the current Middle East crisis, some countries did restrict exports of essential goods. There is a certain rationality to political decisions aimed at protecting one’s own economy. But if every country were to take similar measures, importing nations would find procurement increasingly difficult, and cross-border supply chain disruption would deepen. Preventing this outcome requires international cooperation in building supply chain resilience.

Moreover, in today’s world with an advanced international division of labor, a shortage of critical materials in one country ripples through the production activities of others. Takaichi noted in her Hanoi address that a cut-off in crude oil supplies to Southeast Asian nations would also halt exports of chemical products to countries across Asia. As a response to these risks, Japan announced in April 2026 “POWERR Asia,” a package of approximately $10 billion in financial cooperation to help Asian countries’ procure crude oil and petroleum products and develop stockpiling systems. The prime minister framed this as a concrete embodiment of the Updated FOIP.

WTO rules do regulate, under certain conditions, export restrictions by member states. But there are challenges, such as securing alternative supplies in a crisis and responding to economic coercion, that existing rules alone cannot fully address. Efforts to fill these gaps through regional trade agreements are gaining momentum. Negotiations are underway to amend the CPTPP with a view to strengthening supply chain resilience; there are also indications that participating countries intend to deepen dialogue and cooperation in responding to economic coercion and market-distorting practices. Within RCEP, attention is being directed at addressing new challenges, including supply chain resilience, ahead of the agreement’s scheduled review in 2027.

International cooperation is equally indispensable in the digital domain. The misuse of generative AI is accelerating and scaling up cyberattacks. As the critical infrastructure of different countries becomes ever more interconnected, the damage from cyberattacks can spread across borders. Takaichi has proposed the “FOIP Digital Corridor Concept,” with trusted communications infrastructure at its center. Japan has long invested in capacity building in this area, including through the ASEAN-Japan Cybersecurity Capacity Building Centre (AJCCBC). Beyond diversifying communications routes, it will also be important to strengthen the capabilities of all countries through threat information sharing and joint exercises.

What, then, does effective regional cooperation require if it is to be genuinely meaningful for the countries of the region? The “ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific” (AOIP) places the emphasis on openness, inclusivity, and ASEAN centrality. The 2025 Japan-ASEAN Joint Statement confirmed that the AOIP and FOIP share fundamental principles. But sharing principles is a different matter from ensuring that concrete cooperation serves the interests of both sides. In energy cooperation, for instance, the test is whether it actually leads to diversification of ASEAN member states’ procurement sources and enhanced stockpiling capacity.

What matters most is not the creation of new frameworks but the accumulation of real results. The success or failure of the Updated FOIP should be measured not by the number of projects or frameworks, but by the degree to which Japan and its partner countries have been able to expand their economic options and reduce their vulnerability to supply disruptions and similar shocks.
